paragraphs.text: This oolong was grown in [Nantou](nantou:where-it-is), the county in the middle of Taiwan and the only one that does not touch the sea. It holds more than half of the island's tea plantings, and its tea country is [divided by height](nantou:altitude-bands), from low hills to cool, misty gardens above about a thousand metres. The county name alone does not say which of those belts a tea grew in.

The leaf was made as [GABA oolong](gaba:definition), which names a way of making tea, not a plant or a place. The fresh leaf is held for some hours [without oxygen](gaba:making), and Taiwan's method alternates those rounds with rounds in air. With no oxygen, the leaf turns its glutamic acid into GABA and cannot break it down again, so the GABA builds up. After that it is made like any [oolong](oolong:definition): withered and tossed, fixed, rolled and dried. The method was [found in Japan](gaba:history) in 1987, and Taiwan's tea research station adapted it to oolong.
At two years it is a young tea. In Taiwan's tradition of keeping [old tea](taiwan-oolong:ageing), those who give a figure for when an oolong becomes old put it between ten and thirty years.

brewing.text: In a cup or pot, steep it for about two to five minutes. It is forgiving of small changes in water temperature and steeping time. It can also be cold-brewed, steeped for some hours in the fridge.

notice.text: Ripe, dried or stewed fruit such as apricot, honeyed sweetness, a smooth, round body, and little bitterness or astringency; often brown sugar or roasted grain, sometimes wood or spice, and a light fruity sourness.
